workEn: The Four Branches of the Mabinogi
title: Branwen uerch Lyr
titleEn: Branwen, Daughter of Llŷr — Branwen given to Matholwch
source: Pedeir Keinc y Mabinogi, Second Branch, from the White Book of Rhydderch (NLW Peniarth 4, c. 1350) as printed in J. Gwenogvryn Evans, The White Book Mabinogion (Pwllheli, 1907), columns 38–47; public domain. Readings are the manuscript's as Evans prints them, checked against the page images; word division, punctuation, capitals and quotation marks are ours. Where the White Book omits a word the sense requires, it is supplied from the Red Book (Rhŷs & Evans) and the note says so. Pronunciation convention: the manuscript spelling read with the sounds of Welsh c. 1300. Translations made fresh from the Welsh.

sentences.t: Bendigeiduran uab Llyr a oed urenhin coronawc ar yr ynys hon, ac ardyrchawc o goron Lundein.
sentences.l: Bendigeidfran son of-Llŷr it-was-that was crowned king over this island, and exalted with the crown of-London.
sentences.i: Bendigeidfran son of Llŷr was crowned king over this island, and exalted with the crown of London.
sentences.n: The Second Branch opens with the tale's ordinary order: subject first, then the particle a, then the verb (a oed 'was') — the 'abnormal sentence', which stresses nothing and is simply how this prose is built. Bendigeiduran is Bendigeid 'blessed' + bran, softened to uran (u = v, modern f): modern Bendigeidfran. uab ← mab 'son', softened after a name; Llyr is modern Llŷr. urenhin ← brenhin 'king', softened as the complement of oed. ar yr ynys hon 'over this island' is Britain. ardyrchawc 'exalted, splendid'. o goron ← coron 'crown', softened after o; Lundein ← Llundein (Llundain), 'London', softened after the feminine noun coron.

sentences.t: A frynhawngueith yd oed yn Hardlech yn Ardudwy, yn llys idaw.
sentences.l: And one-afternoon he-was at Harlech in Ardudwy, at a court to-him.
sentences.i: And one afternoon he was at Harlech in Ardudwy, at a court of his.
sentences.n: A frynhawngueith 'and one afternoon': prynhawn 'afternoon' + gweith 'time', with the spirant mutation after a 'and' (p > ph); the scribe writes the ph sound as f (the Red Book has a phrynhawngweith). Compare A threigylgweith 'and once' in the First Branch. yd oed 'he was': the particle yd comes before the verb when something other than the subject opens the sentence. Hardlech is Harlech (hardd 'fair' + llech 'slab of rock'; d = dd); Ardudwy is the cantref it stands in. yn llys idaw 'in a court to him' = at one of his courts; idaw 'to him' is the preposition y conjugated.

sentences.t: Ac yn eisted yd oedynt ar garrec Hardlech, uch penn y weilgi, a Manawydan uab Llyr y urawt y gyt ac ef, a deu uroder un uam ac ef, Nissyen ac Efnyssen, a guyrda y am hynny, mal y gwedei ynghylch brenhin.
sentences.l: And sitting they-were on the rock of-Harlech, above the head of the sea, and Manawydan son of-Llŷr his brother together with him, and two brothers of-one mother with him, Nisien and Efnysien, and noblemen besides that, as was-fitting around a king.
sentences.i: And they were sitting on the rock of Harlech, above the sea, with Manawydan son of Llŷr, his brother, beside him, and two brothers by the same mother as he, Nisien and Efnysien, and noblemen besides, as was fitting about a king.
sentences.n: Ac yn eisted yd oedynt 'and sitting they were': the verbal phrase is put first, so the verb takes yd. ar garrec ← carrec 'rock', softened after ar. uch penn y weilgi 'above the head of the sea': gweilgi is a poet's word for the open sea, softened after the feminine article. y urawt ← brawt 'his brother', softened after y 'his'. y gyt ac ef 'together with him'. deu uroder ← broder 'brothers', softened after deu 'two'; un uam ← mam, softened after un: 'of one mother with him' — half-brothers through their mother, as the next sentence explains. Nissyen and Efnyssen (ss for s) are modern Nisien and Efnysien. guyrda 'noblemen' (gwyr 'men' + da 'good'); y am hynny 'besides that'. mal y gwedei 'as was fitting', the imperfect of gweddu. ynghylch 'around' is yn + kylch with the nasal mutation.

sentences.t: Y deu uroder un uam ac ef, meibon oedynt y Eurosswyd o'e uam ynteu Penardim, uerch Ueli uab Mynogan.
sentences.l: The two brothers of-one mother with him, sons they-were to Euroswydd by his mother his-own, Penardim, daughter of-Beli son of-Mynogan.
sentences.i: The two brothers by his mother were sons of Euroswydd by Bendigeidfran's own mother, Penardim, daughter of Beli son of Mynogan.
sentences.n: The topic is set out first (Y deu uroder …) and then the sentence proper: meibon oedynt 'sons they were', predicate before verb. y Eurosswyd 'to Euroswydd' (ss for s, d = dd). o'e uam is o 'of, by' + 'e 'his' + mam, softened after 'e; ynteu after it marks 'his own', Bendigeidfran's mother as against Euroswydd's. Penardim is the name as both manuscripts write it here — the White Book and the Red Book alike; later editors print Penarddun, but this edition keeps Penardim in the English as well. uerch Ueli ← merch Beli: merch is softened after the name before it, and Beli after the feminine merch. Beli son of Mynogan is the legendary ancestor-king of the Britons.

sentences.t: A'r neill o'r gueisson hynny, gwas da oed: ef a barei tangneued y rwg y deu lu, ban uydynt lidyawcaf: sef oed hwnnw Nissyen.
sentences.l: And the one of those lads, a good lad he-was: he it-was-that would-make peace between the two hosts, when they-would-be angriest: that-is who that-one was, Nisien.
sentences.i: One of those young men was a good youth: he would make peace between two hosts when they were at their angriest. That one was Nisien.
sentences.n: A'r neill 'and the one (of two)'. gueisson is the plural of gwas 'youth, lad'. gwas da oed: predicate first again. ef a barei ← parei, the imperfect of peri 'cause', softened after a; the imperfect here is habitual, 'he would make'. tangneued 'peace' (modern tangnefedd). y rwg is a spelling of y rwng 'between' (the next sentence has rwng). y deu lu ← llu 'host', softened after deu: 'the two hosts' means any two hosts at odds. ban uydynt 'when they would be': ban 'when', uydynt ← bydynt, the habitual imperfect of bot, softened after ban (= pan 'when'). lidyawcaf ← llidyawcaf, superlative of llidyawc 'angry', softened as the complement. sef oed hwnnw Nissyen 'that is, that one was Nisien': sef names the answer.

sentences.t: Y llall a barei ymlad y rwng y deu uroder, ban uei uwyaf yd ymgerynt.
sentences.l: The other it-was-that would-cause fighting between the two brothers, when it-would-be most that they-loved-each-other.
sentences.i: The other would set two brothers fighting just when they loved each other best.
sentences.n: Y llall 'the other' — the brother not named here is Efnysien. a barei 'would cause', as above, with the verbal noun ymlad 'fighting'. y deu uroder 'the two brothers': as with y deu lu, any two brothers, not a particular pair. ban uei 'when it would be': uei ← bei, the imperfect subjunctive of bot, softened after ban. uwyaf ← mwyaf 'most'. yd ymgerynt 'that they loved one another': the imperfect of ymgaru, the reciprocal prefix ym- + caru 'love', with the a turned to e by the ending.

sentences.t: Ac ual yd oedynt yn eisted yuelly, wynt a welynt teir llong ar dec, yn dyuot o deheu Iwerdon, ac yn kyrchu parth ac attunt, a cherdet rugyl ebrwyd ganthunt, y gwynt yn eu hol, ac yn nessau yn ebrwyd attunt.
sentences.l: And as they-were sitting thus, they it-was-that saw thirteen ships, coming from the south of-Ireland, and making towards them, and a going easy swift with-them, the wind behind-them, and drawing-near swiftly to-them.
sentences.i: And as they sat there so, they saw thirteen ships coming from the south of Ireland and making towards them, running easily and swiftly with the wind behind them, and fast drawing near.
sentences.n: yuelly 'thus, so'. wynt a welynt 'they saw': the abnormal sentence with the imperfect of gwelet. teir llong ar dec 'three ships on ten' = thirteen: teir is the feminine of tri, since llong is feminine; dec is deg (-c for -g). deheu Iwerdon 'the south of Ireland'. parth ac attunt 'towards them': attunt is at 'to' conjugated, third person plural. a cherdet ← kerdet 'going', with the spirant mutation after a; rugyl 'easy, free' (rhugl) and ebrwyd 'swift' describe it; ganthunt 'with them' is gan conjugated. yn eu hol 'in their track' = behind them: eu 'their' puts h before the vowel of ol. nessau 'draw near'.

sentences.t: “Mi a welaf longeu racco,” heb y brenhin, “ac yn dyuot yn hy parth a'r tir.
sentences.l: “I it-is-that see ships yonder,” said the king, “and coming boldly towards the land.
sentences.i: “I see ships out there,” said the king, “and they are coming boldly towards the land.
sentences.n: Mi a welaf 'I see', the abnormal sentence in speech. longeu ← llongeu 'ships', softened as the object. racco 'yonder, over there'. heb y brenhin 'said the king': heb is the defective verb used only to tag speech. yn hy 'boldly': hy 'bold' with the adverbial yn. parth a'r tir 'towards the land'.

sentences.t: Ac erchwch y wyr y llys wiscaw amdanunt, a mynet y edrych pa uedwl yw yr eidunt.”
sentences.l: And bid the men of the court to-dress about-them, and to-go to look what intention is theirs.”
sentences.i: Bid the men of the court arm themselves, and go and see what they intend.”
sentences.n: erchwch is the plural imperative of erchi 'ask, bid'. y wyr ← gwyr 'men', softened after y 'to'. wiscaw amdanunt 'to dress about them' (gwiscaw, softened as the object of the bidding): to put on their gear, which before ships of unknown purpose must mean their arms. amdanunt is am 'about' conjugated, third person plural. y edrych 'to look'. pa uedwl ← medwl 'thought, intention', softened after pa 'what'. yr eidunt 'theirs', the independent possessive.

sentences.t: Y gwyr a wiscawd amdanunt ac a nessayssant attunt y wayret.
sentences.l: The men it-was-that dressed about-them and that drew-near to-them downward.
sentences.i: The men armed themselves and went down towards them.
sentences.n: a wiscawd 'dressed' is a third person singular preterite in -awd, the old ending beside -wys: after the relative a the verb may stay singular though the subject is plural. The second verb, a nessayssant 'drew near', is plural (preterite -assant). y wayret 'downwards' (gwaeret 'slope'), down from the rock to the shore.

sentences.t: Gwedy guelet y llongeu o agos, diheu oed ganthunt na welsynt eiryoet llongeu gyweirach eu hansawd noc wy.
sentences.l: After seeing the ships from near, certain it-was with-them that they-had-not-seen ever ships better-arrayed their appearance than they.
sentences.i: When they saw the ships close at hand, they were certain they had never seen ships better fitted out in appearance.
sentences.n: Gwedy guelet 'after seeing' (gu = gw). diheu oed ganthunt 'certain it was with them' = they were sure: what one thinks is 'with' one. na welsynt 'that they had not seen': welsynt is the pluperfect (-synt), a tense modern Welsh has lost. gyweirach is the comparative of kyweir 'well-arrayed, in good order', written softened. eu hansawd 'their appearance': h before the vowel after eu (ansawd). noc wy 'than they': no 'than' takes c before a vowel.

sentences.t: Arwydon tec, guedus, arwreid o bali oed arnunt.
sentences.l: Ensigns fair, seemly, splendid of brocade were on-them.
sentences.i: Fair, seemly, splendid ensigns of brocade were on them.
sentences.n: arwydon 'signs, ensigns', plural of arwyd. tec 'fair' (teg, -c for -g); guedus 'seemly, fitting'. arwreid, from arwr 'hero', is 'heroic, splendid'; the Red Book has no word here (arwydon tec gwedus o bali). o bali ← pali 'brocade', a rich silk, softened after o. oed 'was', singular after the plural subject that comes first; arnunt 'on them'.

sentences.t: Ac ar hynny, nachaf un o'r llongeu yn raculaenu rac y rei ereill, ac y guelynt dyrchauael taryan yn uch no bwrd y llong, a swch y taryan y uynyd yn arwyd tangneued.
sentences.l: And at that, behold one of the ships out-going-ahead before the others, and they-saw raising a shield higher than the board of the ship, and the point of the shield upward as a sign of peace.
sentences.i: And with that, one of the ships drew out ahead of the others, and they saw a shield raised above the ship's side, its point upward as a sign of peace.
sentences.n: Ac ar hynny 'and at that, thereupon'. nachaf 'behold' (like llyma) sets the scene before the eyes, with a verbal noun following. raculaenu is rac 'before' + blaenu 'go first', softened in the compound (b > u): 'outstrip, go out ahead'. Evans prints it spaced, rac ulaenu; it is one compound verb. y rei ereill 'the others'. y guelynt 'they saw', imperfect. dyrchauael 'raising' (dyrchafael). yn uch no 'higher than'. bwrd y llong 'the ship's board', its side. swch 'point', literally a ploughshare; y uynyd 'upward' (mynyd 'mountain', softened). yn arwyd 'as a sign': predicative yn.

sentences.t: Ac y nessawys y gwyr attunt, ual yd ymglywynt ymdidan.
sentences.l: And the men drew-near to-them, so-that they-could-hear-each-other talk.
sentences.i: And the men drew near to them, until each side could hear the other speak.
sentences.n: y nessawys 'drew near': verb first, with the particle y; the -wys preterite stays singular before the plural subject y gwyr, who are the king's men gone down to the shore. ual 'so that'. yd ymglywynt 'they could hear one another': the reciprocal ym- + clywet 'hear', imperfect plural. ymdidan 'talk, conversation'.

sentences.t: Bwrw badeu allan a wnaethont wynteu, a nessau parth a'r tir, a chyuarch guell y'r brenhin.
sentences.l: Putting boats out they-did they-for-their-part, and drawing-near towards the land, and greeting to the king.
sentences.i: They for their part put out boats, came in towards the land, and greeted the king.
sentences.n: Bwrw badeu allan a wnaethont 'putting boats out they did': a verbal noun, then a, then a form of gwneuthur 'do' — the narrative pattern that means simply 'they put out boats'. wnaethont is a spelling of wnaethant (the Red Book has wnaethant). wynteu 'they for their part' marks the turn to the men in the ships. badeu 'boats', plural of bad. a chyuarch guell 'and greeting': kyuarch gwell, literally 'ask better', with the spirant mutation after a. y'r 'to the'.

sentences.t: E brenhin a'e clywei wynteu o'r lle yd oed ar garrec uchel uch eu penn.
sentences.l: The king it-was-that heard-them them-for-their-part from the place he-was on a high rock above their head.
sentences.i: The king could hear them from where he was, on the high rock above their heads.
sentences.n: E brenhin: E is a spelling of the article y. a'e clywei 'heard them': the infixed pronoun 'e 'them' stands between the particle a and the verb; clywei is the imperfect. o'r lle yd oed 'from the place that he was'. garrec ← carrec, softened after ar; uchel 'high'. uch eu penn 'above their head': Welsh keeps the singular for a part each person has one of.

sentences.t: “Duw a rodo da ywch,” heb ef, “a grayssaw wrthywch.
sentences.l: “God may-he-give good to-you,” said he, “and welcome to-you.
sentences.i: “God give you good,” he said, “and welcome to you.
sentences.n: Duw a rodo 'may God give': rodo is the present subjunctive of rodi, the mood of wishing, as in Duw a dalo 'may God repay'. ywch 'to you', plural (y conjugated). grayssaw 'welcome' (modern croeso) is the word's own form, not a mutation. wrthywch 'towards you', wrth conjugated: welcome is given 'towards' a person.

sentences.t: Pieu yniuer y llongeu hynn, a phwy yssyd pennaf arnunt wy?”
sentences.l: Whose is the company of these ships, and who is chiefest over-them they?”
sentences.i: Whose is the company in these ships, and who is chief over them?”
sentences.n: Pieu 'whose is?' (modern piau). yniuer 'company, host' (niuer with a prefixed y). a phwy 'and who', spirant after a. yssyd 'who is', the relative form of bot. pennaf 'chief', the superlative of penn 'head'. arnunt wy 'over them', ar conjugated with the echoing pronoun.

sentences.t: “Arglwyd,” heb wynt, “mae ymma Matholwch brenhin Iwerdon, ac ef bieu y llongeu.”
sentences.l: “Lord,” said they, “there-is here Matholwch king of-Ireland, and he owns the ships.”
sentences.i: “Lord,” they said, “Matholwch, king of Ireland, is here, and the ships are his.”
sentences.n: heb wynt 'said they'. mae ymma 'is here': mae, the 'is' that opens a statement of where something is. ef bieu y llongeu 'he owns the ships': bieu 'owns' always follows its subject, a relic of an old relative construction.

sentences.t: “Beth,” heb y brenhin, “a uynnhei ef?
sentences.l: “What,” said the king, “would-he-want?
sentences.i: “What,” said the king, “would he want?
sentences.n: Beth … a uynnhei ef 'what would he want': the question word comes first, then the relative a. uynnhei ← mynnhei, the imperfect of mynnu 'want', softened after a; the scribe writes the n + h of mynnu as nnh. The imperfect is the courteous 'would'.

sentences.t: A uyn ef dyuot y'r tir?”
sentences.l: Does-he-want to-come to the land?”
sentences.i: Does he wish to come ashore?”
sentences.n: A uyn ef: A is the question particle, and it softens the verb: uyn ← myn, the present of mynnu. dyuot y'r tir 'to come to the land', to come ashore.

sentences.t: “Na uynn, Arglwyd,” heb wynt, “negessawl yw wrthyt ti, onyt y neges a geif.”
sentences.l: “He-does-not-want, Lord,” said they, “having-an-errand he-is to-you, unless his errand he-gets.”
sentences.i: “He does not, Lord,” they said; “he has come on an errand to you, and not unless his errand is granted.”
sentences.n: Na uynn 'wants not': Welsh answers by repeating the verb, here negated with na, which softens it. negessawl 'having an errand' (neges 'errand, business' + the adjective ending -awl). wrthyt ti 'to you', wrth conjugated. onyt 'unless, if not'. y neges a geif 'his errand he gets': the object first, then a; geif ← keif, the present of kaffael 'get', softened after a. The answer joins two thoughts: he will not come ashore, and he will not come unless his errand is granted.

sentences.t: “By ryw neges yw yr eidaw ef?” heb y brenhin.
sentences.l: “What kind-of errand is his?” said the king.
sentences.i: “What manner of errand is his?” said the king.
sentences.n: By ryw 'what kind of': by is a spelling of py, pa 'what', and ryw ← rhyw 'kind', softened after it. yr eidaw ef 'his', the independent possessive (eiddo).

sentences.t: “Mynnu ymgyuathrachu a thidy, Arglwyd,” heb wynt.
sentences.l: “Wanting to-ally-himself-by-marriage with you, Lord,” said they.
sentences.i: “He wishes to ally himself with you by marriage, Lord,” they said.
sentences.n: Mynnu 'wanting': a verbal noun answers the question, the subject understood. ymgyuathrachu 'to become kin by marriage', from kyuathrach 'kinship by marriage', with the reciprocal ym-. a thidy 'with you': a 'with' and the spirant mutation, t > th; tidy is the doubled, emphatic 'you'.

sentences.t: “Y erchi Branwen uerch Lyr y doeth, ac os da genhyt ti, ef a uyn ymrwymaw Ynys y Kedeirn ac Iwerdon y gyt, ual y bydynt gadarnach.”
sentences.l: “To ask-for Branwen daughter of-Llŷr he-came, and if good with-you, he it-is-that wants to-bind the Island of the Mighty and Ireland together, so-that they-would-be stronger.”
sentences.i: “He has come to ask for Branwen daughter of Llŷr; and if it please you, he wishes to bind the Island of the Mighty and Ireland together, so that both may be the stronger.”
sentences.n: Y erchi Branwen … y doeth 'to ask for Branwen he came': the purpose is put first, so the verb takes y. uerch Lyr ← merch Llyr, as uerch Ueli above. os da genhyt ti 'if it is good with you', if you please. ef a uyn 'he wants'. ymrwymaw 'bind together'. Ynys y Kedeirn 'the Island of the Mighty' is Britain: kedeirn is the plural of kadarn 'mighty'. ual y bydynt 'so that they would be': bydynt is the habitual imperfect of bot, as ban uydynt in the opening paragraph. gadarnach ← kadarnach 'stronger', softened as the complement.

sentences.t: “Ie,” heb ynteu, “doet y'r tir, a chynghor a gymerwn ninheu am hynny.”
sentences.l: “Yes,” said he-for-his-part, “let-him-come to the land, and counsel we it-is-that will-take we-for-our-part about that.”
sentences.i: “Yes,” he said, “let him come ashore, and we shall take counsel about it.”
sentences.n: heb ynteu 'said he for his part': ynteu marks the change of speaker. doet 'let him come', the third person imperative of dyuot. a chynghor a gymerwn 'and counsel we will take': here the object stands first, then a; chynghor ← kynghor with the spirant after a, gymerwn ← kymerwn, first person plural present of kymryt, softened after a. ninheu 'we for our part'.

sentences.t: Yr atteb hwnnw a aeth ataw ef.
sentences.l: That answer it-was-that went to-him.
sentences.i: That answer went to him.
sentences.n: a aeth 'went', preterite of mynet. ataw 'to him', at conjugated. ef echoes the pronoun.

sentences.t: “Minheu a af yn llawen,” heb ef.
sentences.l: “I-for-my-part it-is-that go gladly,” said he.
sentences.i: “I will go gladly,” he said.
sentences.n: Minheu 'I for my part', the conjunctive pronoun, answering the king. a af 'go, will go': af is the first person present of mynet, which serves for the future too. yn llawen 'gladly'.

sentences.t: Ef a doeth y'r tir, a llawen uuwyt wrthaw; a dygyuor mawr uu yn y llys y nos honno, y rwng e yniuer ef ac yniuer y llys.
sentences.l: He it-was-that came to the land, and glad there-was-being towards-him; and a great mustering was in the court that night, between his company and the company of the court.
sentences.i: He came ashore, and was gladly received; and there was a great gathering in the court that night, of his company and the company of the court.
sentences.n: Ef a doeth 'he came'. llawen uuwyt wrthaw 'glad there was being towards him' = he was made welcome: uuwyt ← buwyt, the impersonal preterite of bot (the -wyt ending), softened as after the relative a, which is left unwritten after the adjective put first (as uu in the next clause). wrthaw 'towards him'. dygyuor 'muster, gathering'. uu ← bu 'was', softened as after a relative a left unwritten. e yniuer ef 'his company': e for y 'his', and ef echoing it; Evans prints eyniuer as one word.

sentences.t: Yn y lle trannoeth, kymryt kynghor.
sentences.l: In the place the-next-day, taking counsel.
sentences.i: At once, the next day, they took counsel.
sentences.n: Yn y lle 'in the place' = at once, straightway. trannoeth 'the next day'. kymryt kynghor 'taking counsel': a verbal noun stands as the whole sentence, with no finite verb at all; the reader supplies 'they'.

sentences.t: Sef a gahat yn y kynghor, rodi Branwen y Uatholwch.
sentences.l: That-is what was-got in the counsel: giving Branwen to Matholwch.
sentences.i: The council resolved to give Branwen to Matholwch.
sentences.n: Sef 'that is': it introduces the answer to an implied question — what did they decide? a gahat 'that was got': kahat, the impersonal preterite of kaffael 'get', softened after a; what is 'got' in council is its outcome. rodi 'giving'. y Uatholwch 'to Matholwch', softened after y 'to' (m > u).

sentences.t: A honno oed tryded prif rieni yn yr ynys hon; teccaf morwyn yn y byt oed.
sentences.l: And she was the-third chief ancestress in this island; the fairest maiden in the world she-was.
sentences.i: And she was one of the Three Chief Ancestresses of this island; she was the fairest maiden in the world.
sentences.n: honno 'that one', feminine. tryded 'third' is the way the Triads speak: 'the third' of a set of three, so one of three. prif rieni is uncertain: rieni normally means 'parents, ancestors'; some take the word here for rianed 'maidens', which would make her one of the 'three chief maidens'. The Red Book has the same words. The reading 'ancestress' is kept, with that doubt. teccaf morwyn 'fairest maiden': the superlative stands before the noun, and the sentence ends on oed 'she was'.

sentences.t: A gwneuthur oed yn Aberfraw y gyscu genti, ac odyno y kychwyn.
sentences.l: And making an-appointment at Aberffraw to sleep with-her, and from-there the setting-out.
sentences.i: And a time was appointed at Aberffraw for him to sleep with her, and to set out from there.
sentences.n: gwneuthur oed 'making an appointment': oed here is not 'was' but the noun oed (oet) 'appointed time, tryst', as in the First Branch's y mae oet y rof i ac ef; the Red Book spells it oet. Aberfraw is Aberffraw in Anglesey, the chief court of Gwynedd (the scribe writes a single f for ff). y gyscu ← kyscu 'sleep', softened after y 'to'. genti 'with her', gan conjugated for a woman. odyno 'from there'. y kychwyn 'the setting out': kychwyn is not softened, so y is the article rather than 'his'.

sentences.t: Ac y kychwynassant yr yniueroed hynny parth ac Aberfraw, Matholwch a'y yniueroed yn y llongheu, Bendigeituran a'y niuer ynteu ar tir, yny doethant hyt yn Aberfraw.
sentences.l: And set-out those hosts towards Aberffraw, Matholwch and his hosts in the ships, Bendigeidfran and his company for-his-part on land, until they-came as-far-as to Aberffraw.
sentences.i: And those companies set out for Aberffraw, Matholwch and his men in the ships and Bendigeidfran and his on land, until they came to Aberffraw.
sentences.n: y kychwynassant 'set out': verb first with the particle y, third person plural preterite in -assant. parth ac 'towards' (ac before a vowel). a'y is a 'and' + y 'his'. llongheu 'ships', written with h (as the scribe writes nnh in mynnhei). Bendigeituran: the scribe also writes the name with t. niuer 'company'; ynteu 'he for his part' sets Bendigeidfran against Matholwch. ar tir 'on land': after ar one expects dir, but the phrase is written unsoftened in both manuscripts. yny doethant 'until they came'; hyt yn 'as far as'.

sentences.t: Yn Aberfraw dechreu y wled, ac eisted.
sentences.l: In Aberffraw beginning the feast, and sitting.
sentences.i: At Aberffraw the feast began, and they sat down.
sentences.n: Two verbal nouns carry the sentence: dechreu 'beginning', eisted 'sitting'. y wled ← gwled 'feast', softened after the feminine article.

sentences.t: Sef ual yd eistedyssant: brenhin Ynys y Kedeirn a Manawydan uab Llyr o'r neill parth idaw, a Matholwch o'r parth arall, a Branwen uerch Lyr gyt ac ynteu.
sentences.l: That-is how they-sat: the king of-the-Island of the Mighty and Manawydan son of-Llŷr on the one side to-him, and Matholwch on the other side, and Branwen daughter of-Llŷr together with him-for-his-part.
sentences.i: The king of the Island of the Mighty sat with Manawydan son of Llŷr on one side of him and Matholwch on the other, and Branwen daughter of Llŷr beside Matholwch.
sentences.n: Sef ual 'that is how'. yd eistedyssant 'they sat', preterite plural in -yssant. o'r neill parth idaw … o'r parth arall 'on the one side of him … on the other side', the phrase the First Branch uses for Pwyll's seating. gyt ac ynteu 'together with him for his part': ynteu points to the last man named, Matholwch, so Branwen sits by her husband-to-be.

sentences.t: Nyt ymywn ty yd oydynt, namyn ymywn palleu.
sentences.l: Not in a house they-were, but in pavilions.
sentences.i: They were not in a house, but in pavilions.
sentences.n: Nyt negates the phrase put first: 'not in a house (it was that) they were'. ymywn 'inside' (y mywn). oydynt is a spelling of oedynt 'they were'. namyn 'but, except'. palleu 'pavilions, tents', plural of pall.

sentences.t: Ny angassei Uendigeituran eiryoet ymywn ty.
sentences.l: Had-not-fitted Bendigeidfran ever inside a house.
sentences.i: No house had ever been able to hold Bendigeidfran.
sentences.n: Ny angassei 'had not been contained, had not fitted': the pluperfect (-assei) of a verb meaning 'have room, be held' (the Red Book writes eyngassei). Uendigeituran is the subject, softened after the verb, as a subject sometimes is in Middle Welsh. eiryoet 'ever'. The tale says it without comment: Bendigeidfran is a giant.

sentences.t: A'r gyuedach a dechreussant.
sentences.l: And the carousing it-was-that they-began.
sentences.i: And they began the carousing.
sentences.n: The object comes first, then a and the verb. gyuedach ← kyuedach 'carousing', the drinking after a meal, softened after the article (it is feminine). dechreussant 'they began', preterite plural of dechreu.

sentences.t: Dilit y gyuedach a wnaethant ac ymdidan.
sentences.l: Pursuing the carousing they-did, and conversing.
sentences.i: They kept up the carousing and the talk.
sentences.n: Dilit … a wnaethant 'pursuing they did': dilit (dilyd, -t for -d) 'follow, keep on with', with the gwneuthur pattern. ac ymdidan 'and conversing' follows after the verb.

sentences.t: A phan welsant uot yn well udunt kymryt hun no dilyt kyuedach, y gyscu yd aethant.
sentences.l: And when they-saw being better for-them to-take sleep than to-pursue carousing, to sleep they-went.
sentences.i: And when they saw that it was better for them to sleep than to carry on carousing, they went to bed.
sentences.n: pan welsant 'when they saw', preterite. uot ← bot 'being', softened as the object: 'that it was'. udunt 'for them', y conjugated. kymryt hun 'take sleep'. no 'than'. y gyscu yd aethant 'to sleep they went': the purpose first, then yd and the verb.

sentences.t: A'r nos honno y kyscwys Matholwch gan Uranwen.
sentences.l: And that night slept Matholwch with Branwen.
sentences.i: And that night Matholwch slept with Branwen.
sentences.n: y kyscwys 'slept', preterite in -wys, verb first after the time phrase. gan Uranwen 'with Branwen', softened after gan (b > u).

sentences.t: A thrannoeth, kyuodi a orugant pawb o niuer y llys; a'r swydwyr a dechreusant ymaruar am rannyat y meirych a'r gweisson.
sentences.l: And next-day, rising they-did, everyone of the company of-the-court; and the officers it-was-that began to-busy-themselves about the allotting of the horses and the lads.
sentences.i: And the next day all the company of the court rose; and the officers set about sharing out lodging for the horses and the grooms.
sentences.n: kyuodi a orugant 'rising they did': orugant is the older plural preterite of gwneuthur; the subject pawb o niuer y llys 'everyone of the court's company' follows. swydwyr 'officers' (swydd 'office'). ymaruar is uncertain in sense; both manuscripts have it, and 'busy themselves with, see to' fits the context. rannyat 'sharing out, allotment' (rhannu 'share'), here of quarters. meirych 'horses', plural of march; gweisson 'lads', here the grooms.

sentences.t: Ac eu rannu a wnaethant ym pob kyueir hyt y mor.
sentences.l: And their sharing they-did into every quarter as-far-as the sea.
sentences.i: And they quartered them in every direction as far as the sea.
sentences.n: eu rannu 'their sharing' = sharing them: the object of a verbal noun is put as a possessive before it. a wnaethant 'they did'. ym pob kyueir 'in every quarter': yn 'in' becomes ym before p (nasal assimilation); kyueir 'region, direction'. hyt y mor 'as far as the sea'.

sentences.t: Ac ar hynny dydgueith, nachaf Efnyssen gwr anagneuedus a dywedassam uchot, yn dywanu y lety meirch Matholwch, a gouyn a wnaeth, pioed y meirch.
sentences.l: And at that one-day, behold Efnysien, the un-peaceable man that we-spoke-of above, chancing to the lodging of-the-horses of-Matholwch, and asking he-did whose-were the horses.
sentences.i: And one day Efnysien, the quarrelsome man we spoke of above, came upon the stabling of Matholwch's horses, and asked whose horses they were.
sentences.n: dydgueith 'one day' (dyd + gweith 'time'). nachaf 'behold' with yn dywanu 'happening, coming by chance'. anagneuedus 'unpeaceable, quarrelsome': an- 'un-' + (t)angneuedus 'peaceable'. a dywedassam uchot 'whom we spoke of above': dywedassam is the first person plural preterite, the storyteller's 'we'; the Red Book adds ni 'we'. y lety ← llety 'lodging', softened after y 'to'. meirch 'horses', the shorter plural beside meirych. a gouyn a wnaeth 'and asking he did'. pioed 'whose was?', the past of pieu.

sentences.t: “Meirych Matholwch brenhin Iwerdon yw y rei hyn,” heb wy.
sentences.l: “Horses of-Matholwch king of-Ireland are these,” said they.
sentences.i: “These are the horses of Matholwch, king of Ireland,” they said.
sentences.n: Predicate first: Meirych Matholwch … yw y rei hyn 'the horses of Matholwch are these'. y rei hyn 'these ones'. heb wy, a spelling of heb wynt 'said they'.

sentences.t: “Beth a wnant wy yna?” heb ef.
sentences.l: “What do they-do they there?” said he.
sentences.i: “What are they doing there?” he said.
sentences.n: Beth a wnant wy 'what do they do': wnant, the present plural of gwneuthur, softened after a. yna 'there'.

sentences.t: “Yma y mae brenhin Iwerdon, ac yr gyscwys gan Uranwen dy chwaer, a'y ueirych yw y rei hynn.”
sentences.l: “Here is the king of-Ireland, and he-has-slept with Branwen your sister, and his horses are these.”
sentences.i: “The king of Ireland is here, and he has slept with Branwen your sister, and these are his horses.”
sentences.n: Yma y mae 'here is': the place first, then y and mae. yr gyscwys 'has slept': yr is the particle ry, which makes a preterite into a perfect and softens the verb (kyscwys > gyscwys). gan Uranwen, as above. dy chwaer 'your sister'. a'y ueirych 'and his horses' (a + y 'his'; meirych softened after y).

sentences.t: “Ay yuelly y gwnaethant wy am uorwyn kystal a honno, ac yn chwaer y minheu, y rodi heb uyghanyat i?
sentences.l: “Is-it thus they-did they about a maiden as-good as that-one, and a sister to me-for-my-part, her giving without my-permission me?
sentences.i: “Is this what they have done with a maiden so fine as she, and my own sister — given her away without my leave?
sentences.n: Ay 'is it?' — the question particle a with y, asking about the word that follows: 'is it thus that …?'. am uorwyn ← morwyn 'maiden', softened after am. kystal a honno 'as good as she'. yn chwaer y minheu 'as a sister to me myself': predicative yn, and minheu 'I for my part'. y rodi 'her giving' = giving her away. uyghanyat 'my permission': uy 'my' causes the nasal mutation, k > ngh, written gh here: kanyat (caniatâd).

sentences.t: Ny ellynt wy tremic uwy arnaf i,” heb ef.
sentences.l: They-could-not they insult greater upon-me,” said he.
sentences.i: They could have put no greater insult upon me,” he said.
sentences.n: Ny ellynt 'they could not': gallynt, the imperfect plural of gallu, loses its g after ny. tremic 'insult, contempt' (tremyg). uwy ← mwy 'greater', softened. arnaf i 'on me', ar conjugated with the echoing i. The Red Book adds no hwnnw 'than that'.

sentences.t: Ac yn hynny guan y dan y meirych, a thorri y guefleu wrth y danned udunt, a'r clusteu wrth y penneu, a'r rawn wrth y keuyn; ac ny caei graf ar yr amranneu, eu llad wrth yr ascwrn.
sentences.l: And at-that, thrusting under the horses, and cutting the lips at the teeth on-them, and the ears at the heads, and the tails at the back; and where he-could-not-get grip on the eyelids, cutting-them at the bone.
sentences.i: And with that he went in among the horses and cut off their lips at the teeth, their ears at the head and their tails at the rump; and where he could get no grip on the eyelids, he cut them away to the bone.
sentences.n: Ac yn hynny 'and at that'. A run of verbal nouns with no finite verb; the reader supplies 'he'. guan y dan y meirych 'thrusting under the horses': gwanu 'stab, thrust'; the sense is that he went at them with a blade, though the exact picture is not clear. a thorri ← torri 'cut', spirant after a. guefleu 'lips'; danned 'teeth'; udunt 'on them', the disadvantaged party. clusteu 'ears'; rawn 'tail-hair' (rhawn, r for rh); keuyn 'back' (cefn). ny caei 'he could not get': caei is the imperfect of kaffael; after ny one expects chaei, which the Red Book writes. graf ← craf 'grip', softened as object. amranneu 'eyelids'. eu llad 'cutting them': llad is 'strike, cut' as well as 'kill'. ascwrn 'bone'.

sentences.t: A gwneuthur anfuryf ar y meirych yuelly, hyt nat oed rym a ellit a'r meirych.
sentences.l: And making disfigurement on the horses thus, until there-was-not use that could-be-had with the horses.
sentences.i: So he maimed the horses, until there was no use to be made of them.
sentences.n: A gwneuthur anfuryf 'and making disfigurement': anfuryf is an- 'un-' + furyf 'form' (ffurf). hyt nat oed 'so that there was not': nat is 'that not'. rym is uncertain; taken as grym 'power, strength', softened as the subject after nat oed (as in modern nid oes le), in the sense 'use, good'. a ellit 'that could be': ellit ← gellit, the impersonal imperfect of gallu, softened after a.

sentences.t: E chwedyl a doeth at Uatholwch.
sentences.l: The tale it-was-that came to Matholwch.
sentences.i: The news came to Matholwch.
sentences.n: E chwedyl 'the tale, the news' (chwedl): E is the article. at Uatholwch 'to Matholwch', softened after at.

sentences.t: Sef ual y doeth: dywedut anfuruaw y ueirych ac eu llygru, hyt nat oed un mwynyant a ellit ohonunt.
sentences.l: That-is how it-came: saying the disfiguring of-his horses and their spoiling, until there-was-not one benefit that could-be-had from-them.
sentences.i: He was told that his horses had been maimed and spoiled, so that no use at all could be had of them.
sentences.n: Sef ual y doeth 'that is how it came'. dywedut 'telling', a verbal noun with the speaker unnamed. anfuruaw 'disfiguring', the verb from anfuryf. y ueirych ← meirych, softened after y 'his'. eu llygru 'their spoiling' = spoiling them. mwynyant 'benefit, use' (mwyniant). ohonunt 'from them', o conjugated.

sentences.t: “Ie, Arglwyd,” heb un, “dy waradwydaw yr a wnaethpwyt, a hynny a uynhir y wneuthur a thi.”
sentences.l: “Yes, Lord,” said one, “your shaming it-is that has-been-done, and that is-wanted to-do with you.”
sentences.i: “Yes, Lord,” said one, “it is an insult to you that has been done, and that is what they mean to do to you.”
sentences.n: dy waradwydaw 'your shaming' = shaming you: gwaradwydaw 'disgrace, dishonour', softened after dy, the object put as a possessive. The yr that follows is hard: it may be the particle ry (as in yr gyscwys above) before the relative a, 'that has been done'; the Red Book has heb yr un 'said the one' and no yr here, so the White Book's yr may be that article displaced. a wnaethpwyt 'that was done', the impersonal preterite of gwneuthur (-pwyt). a uynhir 'is wanted': mynhir, the impersonal present of mynnu, softened. y wneuthur 'its doing'. a thi 'with you' (the Red Book: ytti 'to you').

sentences.t: “Dioer, eres genhyf, os uy gwaradwydaw a uynhynt, rodi morwyn gystal, kyuurd, gyn anwylet gan y chenedyl, ac a rodyssant ym.”
sentences.l: “Assuredly, strange with-me, if my shaming that they-wanted, to-give a maiden so-good, of-equal-rank, so dear to her kindred, as they-gave to-me.”
sentences.i: “Indeed, I find it strange that, if they meant to shame me, they should give me a maiden so fine, of a rank so equal to mine, and so dear to her kindred, as the one they gave me.”
sentences.n: Dioer 'assuredly', the oath (worn down from Duw a wyr 'God knows'). eres genhyf 'strange with me' = I find it strange. uy gwaradwydaw 'my shaming': after uy 'my' one expects the nasal mutation, ngwaradwydaw, which the scribe does not write here (the Red Book shows it). a uynhynt 'that they wanted', imperfect plural of mynnu. gystal ← kystal 'as good', softened after the feminine morwyn. kyuurd 'of equal rank' (kyf- 'co-' + urdd 'order, rank'). gyn anwylet 'so dear': gyn ← kyn 'as, so', softened like gystal, with the equative of annwyl 'dear'. y chenedyl 'her kindred': y 'her' gives the spirant, k > ch. ac a rodyssant ym 'as they gave to me': ac 'as' after the equatives; ym 'to me'.

sentences.t: “Arglwyd,” heb un arall, “ti a wely dangos ef.
sentences.l: “Lord,” said another, “you it-is-that see showing it.
sentences.i: “Lord,” said another, “you see the proof of it.
sentences.n: ti a wely 'you see': wely ← gwely, the second person present of gwelet, softened after a. dangos ef 'showing it', a verbal noun with its object: you see it shown. The Red Book reads dangos mae ef 'showing that it is so'; the White Book has no mae, and nothing is supplied — the words are construed as printed.

sentences.t: Ac nyt oes it a wnelych namyn kyrchu dy longeu.”
sentences.l: And there-is-not for-you what you-may-do but to-make-for your ships.”
sentences.i: And there is nothing left for you to do but make for your ships.”
sentences.n: nyt oes 'there is not', the negative of existence. it 'for you', y conjugated. a wnelych 'what you may do', the present subjunctive of gwneuthur, second person. namyn 'but, except'. kyrchu 'make for'. dy longeu ← llongeu, softened after dy.

sentences.t: Ac ar hynny arouun y longeu a wnaeth ef.
sentences.l: And at that, setting-out to his ships he-did he.
sentences.i: And with that he set off for his ships.
sentences.n: arouun (modern arofun) 'intend, set out for': a verbal noun with a wnaeth 'he did'. y longeu 'his ships', softened after y 'his', with the sense 'for his ships'.

sentences.t: E chwedyl a doeth at Uendigeituran, bot Matholwch yn adaw y llys, heb ouyn, heb ganhyat.
sentences.l: The news it-was-that came to Bendigeidfran: Matholwch's being leaving the court, without asking, without leave.
sentences.i: The news came to Bendigeidfran that Matholwch was leaving the court without asking and without leave.
sentences.n: E chwedyl a doeth 'the news came', the abnormal sentence again, as at the opening of the branch (doeth, third-person singular preterite of dyuot 'come'). at Uendigeituran 'to Bendigeidfran' ← Bendigeituran, softened after at. bot Matholwch yn adaw 'Matholwch being leaving' = that Matholwch was leaving: bot 'be' introduces reported fact. heb ouyn ← gofyn 'asking', heb ganhyat ← canhyat 'leave', each softened after heb 'without'.

sentences.t: A chenadeu a aeth y ouyn idaw, paham oed hynny.
sentences.l: And messengers it-was-that went to ask of-him why was that.
sentences.i: And messengers went to ask him why this was.
sentences.n: a chenadeu ← kennadeu 'messengers', with the spirant mutation (k > ch) after a 'and'; the scribe writes the word with one n here and with nn in the next sentence. a aeth 'went': a singular verb after a plural subject, normal in the abnormal sentence. y ouyn idaw 'to ask (of) him': gofyn takes y/i 'to' of the person asked, and idaw is y conjugated, third person singular masculine. paham 'why' (pa + achaws, 'for what cause').

sentences.t: Sef kennadeu a aeth, Idic uab Anarawc, ac Eueyd Hir.
sentences.l: That-is the messengers that went: Iddig son of-Anarawg, and Efeydd Hir.
sentences.i: The messengers who went were Iddig son of Anarawg and Efeydd Hir.
sentences.n: Sef 'that is' answers an implied question (which messengers?). Idic uab Anarawc: uab ← mab 'son', softened after a personal name, as in every patronymic; -c = -g (Anarawc = Anarawg). Eueyd Hir is Efeydd Hir, 'Efeydd the Tall' (hir 'long, tall'); he is sent again below.

sentences.t: Y guyr hynny a'y godiwawd, ac a ouynyssant idaw, pa darpar oed yr eidaw, a pha achaws yd oed yn mynet e ymdeith.
sentences.l: Those men it-was-that overtook-him, and that asked of-him what intention was his, and what cause he-was going away.
sentences.i: These men overtook him and asked him what he intended, and for what reason he was going away.
sentences.n: Y guyr hynny a'y godiwawd 'those men overtook him': a'y is the relative a with the infixed object pronoun 'y 'him'; godiwawd ← goddiwes 'overtake', with the old third-person singular preterite ending -awd, singular again after a plural subject. a ouynyssant ← gofynyssant, third-person plural preterite (-yssant). pa darpar 'what purpose': darpar 'preparation, intention' (the radical has d); after pa the softening d > dd is not shown, d being written for both. yr eidaw 'his' (the possessive pronoun, 'that of him'). e ymdeith 'away'.

sentences.t: “Dioer,” heb ynteu, “pei ys gwypwn, ny down yma.
sentences.l: “Assuredly,” said he-for-his-part, “if I-had-known-it, I-would-not-have-come here.
sentences.i: “Indeed,” he said, “had I known it, I would not have come here.
sentences.n: Dioer 'assuredly, indeed', the tale's common oath. heb ynteu 'said he for his part': ynteu marks the change of speaker. pei ys gwypwn 'if I had known it': pei 'if' of an unreal condition; ys is the infixed object 'it', anticipating the whole matter; gwypwn is the imperfect subjunctive of gwybot 'know', first person singular. ny down 'I would not have come': down is the imperfect subjunctive of dyuot (deuwn). Both verbs of an unreal condition take this tense.

sentences.t: Cwbyl waradwyd a geueis.
sentences.l: Complete disgrace it-is-that I-got.
sentences.i: I have been utterly disgraced.
sentences.n: The object comes first and is stressed: Cwbyl waradwyd 'complete disgrace' (gwaradwyd, softened after the adjective cwbyl, which stands before its noun), then a geueis 'I got' ← keueis, first-person singular preterite of kaffael, softened after the particle a. cwbyl = cwbl.

sentences.t: Ac ny duc neb kyrch waeth no'r dugum ymma.
sentences.l: And not brought anyone a-journey worse than-that I-brought here.
sentences.i: And no one ever made a worse journey than the one I have made here.
sentences.n: ny duc neb 'no one brought': duc is the third-person singular preterite of dwyn 'bring, carry', and dugum, its first person, closes the sentence: no'r dugum 'than (that) which I brought'. kyrch is an expedition or errand, the thing one sets out on; dwyn kyrch is 'make a journey'. waeth ← gwaeth 'worse', softened after the noun it follows.

sentences.t: A reuedawt rygyueryw a mi.”
sentences.l: And a-wonder has-befallen me.”
sentences.i: And a strange thing has befallen me.”
sentences.n: reuedawt = ryuedawt 'a wonder, a marvel' (rhyfeddod); r does not mutate after a 'and'. rygyueryw a mi 'has met with me': kyueryw is the third-person singular preterite of kyuaruot 'meet', and the particle ry makes it a perfect ('has met') and softens it, k > g. a mi 'with me'.

sentences.t: “Beth yw hynny?” heb wynt.
sentences.l: “What is that?” said they.
sentences.i: “What is that?” they said.
sentences.n: Beth 'what' (peth 'thing', softened as an interrogative). heb wynt 'said they': heb takes the pronoun after it, as heb ef, heb ynteu.

sentences.t: “Rodi Bronwen uerch Lyr ym, yn tryded prif rieni yr ynys honn, ac yn uerch y urenhin Ynys y Kedeyrn, a chyscu genthi, a gwedy hynny uy gwaradwydaw.
sentences.l: “Giving Branwen daughter of-Llŷr to-me, as the-third chief ancestress of this island, and as daughter to the king of-the-Island of-the-Mighty, and sleeping with-her, and after that my disgracing.
sentences.i: “Branwen daughter of Llŷr was given to me, one of the Three Chief Ancestresses of this island and daughter to the king of the Island of the Mighty, and I slept with her, and after that I was disgraced.
sentences.n: Bronwen: the White Book spells the name so here, once only (Evans prints bron-wen across a line end, and the second witness agrees); everywhere else it is Branwen, and the spelling is kept as written. Rodi … ym 'giving to me' = she was given to me; three verbal nouns tell the story without a finite verb. uerch Lyr 'daughter of Llŷr': Llyr softened after uerch. yn tryded prif rieni: the phrase used of her above, at the council, with the predicative yn, 'as one of the three chief ancestresses'; the sense of rieni here is uncertain ('ancestors, parents', or perhaps for rianed 'maidens'), as noted there. uy gwaradwydaw 'my disgracing': the object of a verbal noun is shown by a possessive before it. Kedeyrn is a spelling of Kedeirn 'the Mighty'.

sentences.t: A ryued oed genhyf, nat kyn rodi morwyn gystal a honno ym, y gwneit y gwaradwyd a wnelit ym.”
sentences.l: And wonder it-was with-me that not before giving a-maiden as-good as that to-me was-done the disgrace that was-done to-me.”
sentences.i: And I wondered that the insult done to me was not done before so fine a maiden was given me.”
sentences.n: ryued oed genhyf 'it was a wonder with me' = I wondered; gan 'with' gives the opinion of a person, and genhyf is gan conjugated, first person singular. nat kyn rodi … y gwneit 'that it was not before the giving … that (it) was done': nat negates the fronted phrase. gwneit and wnelit are impersonals of gwneuthur 'do', the imperfect and the imperfect subjunctive, 'was being done', 'should be done': Middle Welsh has a whole set of these subjectless forms, lost from the modern spoken language. gystal ← kystal 'as good', softened after morwyn, a feminine noun.

sentences.t: “Dioer, Arglwyd, nyt o uod y neb a uedei y llys,” heb wynt, “na neb o'e kynghor y gwnaetpwyt y gwaradwyd hwnnw yt.
sentences.l: “Assuredly, Lord, not by the will of anyone who held the court,” said they, “nor anyone of his council was-done that disgrace to-you.
sentences.i: “Indeed, Lord,” they said, “it was not by the will of anyone who held the court, nor of anyone of his council, that this insult was done you.
sentences.n: y gwnaetpwyt 'was done' is a readable slip for gwnaethpwyt (the Red Book has it with the h), the impersonal preterite of gwneuthur, kept as written; the impersonal -wyt ending (lladdwyd, gwnaethpwyd) is one of the old forms worth learning. nyt o uod 'not of the will': bod 'will, consent', softened after o. a uedei 'who held' ← medei, imperfect of medu 'hold, rule'. o'e kynghor 'of his council' (o + 'e). yt 'to you' = it.

sentences.t: A chyt bo gwaradwyd gennyt ti hynny, mwy yw gan Uendigeituran no chenyt ti, y tremic hwnnw a'r guare.”
sentences.l: And though there-be disgrace with-you you that, greater it-is with Bendigeidfran than with-you, that insult and the sport.”
sentences.i: And though this be a disgrace in your eyes, it is a greater one in Bendigeidfran's than in yours, that insult and that sport.”
sentences.n: chyt bo 'though it be': kyt 'though' (spirant after a) with bo, the present subjunctive of bot. gwaradwyd gennyt ti 'a disgrace with you' = in your estimation; gan again gives the opinion. no chenyt ti 'than with you': spirant mutation after no 'than' (gennyt). y tremic hwnnw a'r guare, 'that insult and the sport', is the subject, held back to the end; tremic is contempt shown, guare (chwarae) a game, here a cruel trick.

sentences.t: “Ie,” heb ef, “mi a tebygaf.
sentences.l: “Yes,” said he, “I it-is-that suppose.
sentences.i: “Yes,” he said, “I believe it.
sentences.n: mi a tebygaf 'I suppose (so)': tebygaf is the first-person singular present of tebygu 'think, suppose'. After the particle a it should be softened to debygaf; the scribe does not show it, and the Red Book (mi atebygaf) does not either. Ie 'yes', assent to what was said.

sentences.t: Ac eissoes ni eill ef uy niwaradwydaw i o hynny.”
sentences.l: And yet he-cannot un-disgrace me of that.”
sentences.i: And yet he cannot clear me of the disgrace of it.”
sentences.n: eissoes 'yet, nevertheless'. ni eill 'cannot', third-person singular present of gallu. uy niwaradwydaw i 'my un-disgracing': diwaradwydaw is di- 'un-' + gwaradwydaw 'disgrace', to take a disgrace away; after uy 'my' it takes the nasal mutation, d > n. o hynny 'of that'.

sentences.t: E gwyr hynny a ymchwelwys a'r atteb hwnnw, parth a'r lle yd oed Uendigeituran, a menegi idaw yr atteb a diwedyssei Uatholwch.
sentences.l: Those men it-was-that returned with that answer, towards the place where Bendigeidfran was, and telling to-him the answer that Matholwch had-said.
sentences.i: The men returned with that answer to where Bendigeidfran was, and told him the answer Matholwch had given.
sentences.n: a ymchwelwys 'returned', third-person singular preterite in -wys after a plural subject. parth a'r lle 'towards the place'. a menegi 'and telling': a verbal noun carries on the narrative. a diwedyssei Uatholwch 'that Matholwch had said': diwedyssei is a form of dywedyssei, the pluperfect (-ssei) of dywedut 'say', and Matholwch is softened after the verb; the Red Book has a rodassei 'had given'.

sentences.t: “Ie,” heb ynteu, “nyt oes ymwaret e uynet ef yn anygneuedus, ac nys gadwn.”
sentences.l: “Yes,” said he-for-his-part, “there-is-not help for his going he in enmity, and we-will-not-allow-it.”
sentences.i: “Yes,” he said, “there is no good in his going away in enmity, and we will not allow it.”
sentences.n: nyt oes ymwaret 'there is no help, no remedy': ymwaret is help or deliverance; the sense here, 'it will not do, it is no good', is drawn from the context. e uynet ef 'his going': e = y 'his', and mynet softened after it, with ef echoing the possessive. yn anygneuedus = yn anagneuedus 'unpeaceably, in enmity' (an- + tangneued 'peace'). nys gadwn 'we will not allow it': ny + the infixed 's 'it'; gadwn is the first-person plural present of gadu 'let'.

sentences.t: “Ie, Arglwyd,” heb wy, “anuon etwa genhadeu yn y ol.”
sentences.l: “Yes, Lord,” said they, “sending again messengers after-him.”
sentences.i: “Yes, Lord,” they said, “send messengers after him again.”
sentences.n: anuon 'sending' (anfon): a bare verbal noun used as a request. etwa 'again, still' (eto). genhadeu ← kennadeu, softened because the adverb etwa stands between it and the verbal noun (an object directly after a verbal noun is not softened); the Red Book has gennadeu too. yn y ol 'in his track', after him.

sentences.t: “Anuonaf,” heb ef.
sentences.l: “I-will-send,” said he.
sentences.i: “I will,” he said.
sentences.n: Anuonaf 'I will send': the first-person singular present (-af) of anuon, which also serves as a future. Welsh answers a request by repeating the verb, not with a word for 'yes'.

sentences.t: “Kyuodwch, Uanawydan uab Llyr, ac Eueyd Hir, ac Unic Glew Yscwyd, ac ewch yn y ol,” heb ef, “a menegwch idaw, ef a geif march iach am pob un o'r a lygrwyt;
sentences.l: “Rise, Manawydan son of-Llŷr, and Efeydd Hir, and Unig Glew Ysgwydd, and go after-him,” said he, “and tell to-him, he it-is-that will-get a-horse sound for every one of-those that were-spoiled;
sentences.i: “Rise, Manawydan son of Llŷr, and Efeydd Hir, and Unig Glew Ysgwydd, and go after him,” he said, “and tell him he shall have a sound horse for every one that was spoiled;
sentences.n: Kyuodwch 'rise' and ewch 'go' are second-person plural imperatives. Uanawydan ← Manawydan, softened as a person addressed. Unic Glew Yscwyd is Unig Glew Ysgwydd, 'Unig Strong Shoulder' (glew 'bold, strong', yscwyd 'shoulder'). menegwch idaw 'tell him', imperative of menegi. am pob un 'for every one': after am one expects bob, which the Red Book writes (am bop); the White Book leaves it unsoftened. ef a geif 'he will get' ← keif, third-person singular present of kaffael, also future. o'r a lygrwyt 'of those that were spoiled': lygrwyt ← llygrwyt, the impersonal preterite (-wyt) of llygru 'spoil, damage'. The king's message runs on through the next three units as one sentence.

sentences.t: ac y gyt a hynny, ef a geif yn wynepwerth idaw llathen aryant a uo kyuref a chyhyt ac ef e hun, a chlawr eur kyflet a'y wyneb, a menegwch ydaw pa ryw wr a wnaeth hynny, a phan yw o'm anuod inheu y gwnaethpwyt hynny;
sentences.l: and together with that, he it-is-that will-get as face-price to-him a-rod of-silver that may-be as-thick and as-long as he himself, and a-plate of-gold as-broad as his face, and tell to-him what kind-of man did that, and that it-is against my-will my-own that was-done that;
sentences.i: and besides that he shall have, as the price of his honour, a rod of silver as thick and as long as himself, and a plate of gold as broad as his face; and tell him what manner of man did this, and that it was done against my will;
sentences.n: wynepwerth 'face-price' (wyneb 'face' + gwerth 'worth') is the payment for an insult to a man's honour, his 'face'; the silver rod and the gold plate measured to his body are the old form of such a payment. a uo 'that may be' (present subjunctive of bot). kyuref a chyhyt 'as thick and as long': kyuref is the equative of praff 'thick', kyhyt of hir 'long' (spirant mutation after a). kyflet a'y wyneb 'as broad as his face': kyflet is the equative of llydan. The second witness adds words here that neither manuscript has, and nothing is supplied. a phan yw 'and that it is': pan here means 'that', introducing what is to be told. o'm anuod inheu 'of my un-will', against my will; inheu is the emphatic 'I for my part'. y gwnaethpwyt 'was done', the impersonal preterite again, here spelled in full.

sentences.t: ac y may brawt un uam a mi a wnaeth hynny, ac nat hawd genhyf i na'e lad na'e diuetha;
sentences.l: and that it-is a-brother of-one mother with me who did that, and that it-is-not easy with-me I either his killing or his destroying;
sentences.i: and that it was a brother of mine by the same mother who did it, and that I cannot easily either kill him or do away with him;
sentences.n: y may brawt … a wnaeth 'that it is a brother … who did': y may = y mae, introducing a reported fact, and then the abnormal sentence with its subject first. un uam a mi 'of one mother with me': mam softened after un 'one', as a feminine noun is. hawd 'easy'. na'e lad na'e diuetha 'either his killing or his destroying': na … na 'neither … nor', and 'e 'his' as the object of each verbal noun; lad ← llad 'kill', softened after 'e 'his'.

sentences.t: a doet y ymwelet a mi,” heb ef, “a mi a wnaf y dangneued ar y llun y mynho e hun.”
sentences.l: and let-him-come to visit with me,” said he, “and I it-is-that will-make the peace in the form that he-may-wish himself.”
sentences.i: and let him come to see me,” he said, “and I will make peace on whatever terms he himself may wish.”
sentences.n: doet 'let him come' is the third-person singular imperative of dyuot. y ymwelet a mi 'to visit with me' (ymweled â). y dangneued 'the peace' ← tangneued, feminine, softened after the article. ar y llun 'in the shape' (llun 'form, figure'): on whatever terms. y mynho 'that he may wish', present subjunctive of mynnu; e hun 'himself'.

sentences.t: E kennadeu a aethant ar ol Matholwch, ac a uanagyssant idaw yr ymadrawd hwnnw yn garedic, ac ef a'e guerendewis.
sentences.l: The messengers it-was-that went after Matholwch, and that told to-him that speech kindly, and he it-was-that listened-to-it.
sentences.i: The messengers went after Matholwch and gave him that message in friendly words, and he listened to it.
sentences.n: a uanagyssant ← managyssant, third-person plural preterite of managu 'tell', the by-form of menegi. yr ymadrawd hwnnw 'that speech' (ymadrodd). yn garedic 'lovingly, kindly' ← karedic, softened after the adverbial yn. a'e guerendewis 'listened to it': the infixed 'e 'it' and guerendewis, third-person singular preterite of gwarandaw 'listen'.

sentences.t: “A wyr,” heb ef, “ni a gymerwn gynghor.”
sentences.l: “O men,” said he, “we it-is-that will-take counsel.”
sentences.i: “Men,” he said, “we shall take counsel.”
sentences.n: A wyr 'O men': gwyr softened after the vocative particle a. ni a gymerwn 'we will take' ← kymerwn, first-person plural present of kymryt, softened after a. gynghor ← kynghor 'counsel', softened as the object.

sentences.t: Ef a aeth yn y gynghor.
sentences.l: He it-was-that went into his council.
sentences.i: He withdrew into council with his men.
sentences.n: yn y gynghor 'into his counsel': kynghor softened after y 'his'. To go into one's council is to withdraw with one's advisers to deliberate.

sentences.t: Sef kynghor a uedylyssant: os gwrthot hynny a wnelynt, bot yn tebygach ganthunt cael kywilid a uei uwy no chael iawn a uei uwy.
sentences.l: That-is the counsel that they-thought: if refusing that they-should-do, being likelier with-them getting shame that would-be greater than getting compensation that would-be greater.
sentences.i: The counsel they reached was that if they refused it, it seemed likelier to them that they would get greater shame than greater compensation.
sentences.n: Sef 'that is' introduces the content of the counsel. a uedylyssant ← medylyssant, third-person plural preterite of medylyaw 'think'. os gwrthot hynny a wnelynt 'if they should refuse that': verbal noun first, then a wnelynt, the imperfect subjunctive (third person plural) of gwneuthur, the mood of a supposed case. bot yn tebygach ganthunt 'being likelier with them': bot reports what they judged; tebygach is the comparative of tebyc 'likely', and ganthunt is gan conjugated, third person plural. iawn 'compensation, redress', the legal word for amends. a uei uwy 'that would be greater': uei is the imperfect subjunctive of bot, softened after a; uwy ← mwy. The Red Book has iawn a vei gymeint 'as great a compensation'.

sentences.t: A disgynnu a wnaeth ar gymryt hynny.
sentences.l: And settling he-did on taking that.
sentences.i: And he made up his mind to accept it.
sentences.n: disgynnu a wnaeth 'alighting he did': a verbal noun, then a wnaeth, the preterite of gwneuthur, makes a past tense ('he settled'). disgynnu ar is to come down on, to settle on a decision. gymryt ← kymryt 'take, accept', softened after ar.

sentences.t: Ac y'r llys y deuthant yn dangneuedus.
sentences.l: And to the court they-came in-peace.
sentences.i: And they came back to the court in peace.
sentences.n: y'r llys 'to the court' comes first, so the verb takes the particle y, not a. deuthant is a third-person plural preterite of dyuot 'come' (doethant elsewhere). yn dangneuedus 'peaceably' ← tangneuedus, softened after the adverbial yn.

sentences.t: A chyweiraw y pebylleu a'r palleu a wnaethant udunt ar ureint kyweirdeb yneuad, a mynet y uwyta.
sentences.l: And arranging the tents and the pavilions they-did for-them after the privilege of-the-arrangement of the hall, and going to eat.
sentences.i: And the tents and pavilions were set out for them as a hall is set out, and they went to eat.
sentences.n: chyweiraw ← kyweiraw 'arrange, make ready', spirant after a. a wnaethant 'they did' closes the verbal-noun clause; its subject is the court's people. udunt 'for them' (y conjugated, third person plural). ar ureint 'in the dignity of', after the manner of: breint softened after ar. kyweirdeb 'arrangement, order'. yneuad is most simply y neuad 'the hall' written together; the Red Book has neuad without the article. y uwyta 'to eat' ← bwyta, softened after y 'to'.

sentences.t: Ac ual y dechreuyssant eisted ar dechreu y wled, yd eistedyssant yna.
sentences.l: And as they-had-begun to-sit at the beginning of-the feast, (so) they-sat then.
sentences.i: And they sat as they had sat when the feast began.
sentences.n: ual y … yd … 'as … so …'. dechreuyssant and eistedyssant are third-person plural preterites (-yssant), the first standing for 'had begun', since Middle Welsh often lets the preterite do the work of the pluperfect. y wled 'the feast' ← gwled, feminine, softened after the article. The seating is the order of the first night.

sentences.t: A dechreu ymdidan a wnaeth Matholwch a Bendigeituran.
sentences.l: And beginning conversing did Matholwch and Bendigeidfran.
sentences.i: And Matholwch and Bendigeidfran began to talk.
sentences.n: dechreu ymdidan a wnaeth 'beginning conversing did': the verbal-noun narrative again, closed by a wnaeth, singular though there are two subjects after it. ymdidan is talk, conversation; the ym- prefix is reciprocal, 'talk with one another'.

sentences.t: Ac nachaf yn ardiawc gan Uendigeituran yn ymdidan, ac yn drist, a gaei gan Uatholwch, a'y lywenyt yn wastat kyn no hynny.
sentences.l: And behold dull with Bendigeidfran in conversing, and sad, what he-got from Matholwch, and his cheer constant before that.
sentences.i: And Bendigeidfran found Matholwch dull company in talk, and sad, though until then he had always been cheerful.
sentences.n: A hard sentence to construe. yn ymdidan is what both manuscripts write (the Red Book likewise); the reading the editors print, yr ymdidan 'the conversation', is their mending, not the text. As written: nachaf 'behold' throws the scene forward; yn ardiawc … ac yn drist 'dull … and sad' describe a gaei gan Uatholwch, 'what he (Bendigeidfran) was getting from Matholwch', and yn ymdidan, 'in conversing', says in what way: Matholwch was heavy and sad in talk. ardiawc is a rare word, taken as 'slow, listless, dull'; its exact sense is uncertain. gaei ← kaei, imperfect of kaffael, softened after a. a'y lywenyt 'and his cheerfulness' ← llywenyt, softened after 'y 'his'. yn wastat 'constant, always'. Before a gaei the Red Book has a further word, printed amywarth (underlined by its editors), whose sense is not clear.

sentences.t: A medylyaw a wnaeth bot yn athrist gan yr unben uychanet a gawssei o iawn am y gam.
sentences.l: And thinking he-did that it-was very-sad with the chieftain how-small what he-had-got of compensation for his wrong.
sentences.i: And he thought that the chieftain was downcast at how little compensation he had received for the wrong done him.
sentences.n: medylyaw a wnaeth 'thinking he did' = he thought; the subject is Bendigeidfran. bot yn athrist 'that it was very sad': athrist is trist 'sad' with the intensive a- (as in athrugar below). gan yr unben 'with the chieftain', in his mind; unben 'chieftain'. uychanet ← bychanet 'how small', the equative (-et) of bychan used as a noun of degree, 'the smallness'; it is written softened. a gawssei 'that he had got' ← kawssei, the pluperfect (-ssei) of kaffael. am y gam 'for his wrong' ← cam, softened after y 'his'.

sentences.t: “A wr,” heb y Bendigeiduran, “nit wyt gystal ymdidanwr heno ac un nos.
sentences.l: “O man,” said Bendigeidfran, “you-are-not as-good a-conversationalist tonight as one night.
sentences.i: “Man,” said Bendigeidfran, “you are not so good a talker tonight as you were the other night.
sentences.n: A wr 'O man' ← gwr, softened after the vocative a. heb y Bendigeiduran: heb before a name takes y, 'said Bendigeidfran'. nit wyt 'you are not'. gystal ← kystal 'as good', softened in the predicate. ymdidanwr 'talker, companion in talk' (ymdidan + -wr 'man'). heno 'tonight'. un nos 'one night', a certain night: the night before.

sentences.t: Ac os yr bychanet genhyt ti dy iawn, ti a gehy ychwanegu yt wrth dy uynnu, ac auory talu dy ueirch yt.”
sentences.l: And if (it is) for the smallness with-you your compensation, you it-is-that will-get increasing to-you according-to your wish, and tomorrow paying your horses to-you.”
sentences.i: And if it is because your compensation seems small to you, you shall have it increased as you please, and tomorrow your horses shall be made good to you.”
sentences.n: os yr bychanet genhyt ti dy iawn 'if (it is) for the smallness, with you, of your compensation': yr = er 'for, because of', and bychanet is the equative of bychan used as a noun, 'the smallness', as in the last sentence but one. ti a gehy 'you will get': gehy is a second-person singular present of kaffael (keffy), softened after a. ychwanegu 'adding, increasing'. wrth dy uynnu 'according to your wishing' (mynnu, softened after dy). talu dy ueirch 'paying your horses' — the horses replaced, a horse for a horse; ueirch ← meirch, softened after dy.

sentences.t: “Arglwyd,” heb ef, “Duw a dalo yt.”
sentences.l: “Lord,” said he, “God may-he-repay to-you.”
sentences.i: “Lord,” he said, “may God repay you.”
sentences.n: Duw a dalo yt 'may God repay you': dalo ← talo, the present subjunctive of talu, softened after a; the subjunctive expresses a wish. yt = it 'to you'. The same thanks recur in every branch and are always given the same English.

sentences.t: “Mi a delediwaf dy iawn heuyt yt,” heb y Bendigeituran.
sentences.l: “I it-is-that will-make-fitting your compensation also to-you,” said Bendigeidfran.
sentences.i: “And I will make your compensation finer still,” said Bendigeidfran.
sentences.n: delediwaf is most likely ← telediwaf, softened after a (t > d): a first-person singular present of a verb made from the adjective telediw 'fair, comely, complete', so 'to make fair, to make complete'; the Red Book has the same form. The verb is rare and its exact sense is not certain; the next sentence shows what he means. heuyt 'also, besides'.

sentences.t: “Mi a rodaf yt peir, a chynnedyf y peir yw, y gwr a lader hediw yt, y uwrw yn y peir, ac erbyn auory y uot yn gystal ac y bu oreu, eithyr na byd llyueryd ganthaw.”
sentences.l: “I it-is-that will-give to-you a-cauldron, and the property of-the cauldron is: the man that-may-be-killed today of-yours, his throwing into the cauldron, and by tomorrow his being as-good as he-was best, except that there-will-not-be speech with-him.”
sentences.i: “I will give you a cauldron, and this is the virtue of the cauldron: if a man of yours is killed today, cast him into the cauldron, and by tomorrow he will be as well as he ever was at his best, save that he will not have the power of speech.”
sentences.n: peir 'cauldron' (pair). kynnedyf 'property, peculiar virtue': the thing a marvellous object can do. y gwr a lader 'the man that may be killed': lader is the impersonal present subjunctive (-er) of llad, softened after a. y uwrw 'his throwing' ← bwrw, softened after y 'his': throw him. erbyn auory 'by tomorrow'. y uot ← bot 'his being'. yn gystal ac y bu oreu 'as good as he was best': goreu softened in the predicate. eithyr 'except'. llyueryd 'speech, utterance': the dead come back dumb.

sentences.t: A diolwch a wnaeth ynteu hyny, a diruawr lywenyd a gymerth ynteu o'r achaws hwnnw.
sentences.l: And thanking he-did he-for-his-part for-that, and huge gladness he-took he-for-his-part from that cause.
sentences.i: And he gave thanks for it, and took great joy in it.
sentences.n: diolwch a wnaeth 'thanking he did' = he thanked. hyny is the White Book's spelling of hynny 'that' here (Evans prints it with a mark over the n, which this edition drops, as it drops all his marks). diruawr 'huge' (dirfawr, di- intensive + mawr) stands before its noun and softens it: lywenyd ← llywenyd 'joy'. a gymerth 'took' ← kymerth, third-person singular preterite of kymryt. o'r achaws hwnnw 'from that cause'.

sentences.t: A thrannoeth y talwyt y ueirych idaw, tra barhawd meirych dof.
sentences.l: And next-day were-paid his horses to-him, while lasted tame horses.
sentences.i: And the next day his horses were made good to him, as long as there were broken horses to give.
sentences.n: y talwyt 'were paid' is the impersonal preterite (-wyt) of talu: no subject is named, the horses are its object. tra barhawd 'while lasted': barhawd ← parhawd, third-person singular preterite (-awd) of parhau, softened after tra 'while'. meirych dof 'tame horses', broken to the saddle; dof does not soften after a plural noun.

sentences.t: Ac odyna y kyrchwyt ac ef kymwt arall, ac y talwyt ebolyon ydaw, yny uu gwbyl idaw y dal.
sentences.l: And from-there was-gone with him another commote, and were-paid colts to-him, until was complete to-him his payment.
sentences.i: And from there he was taken to another commote, and he was paid in colts until his payment was complete.
sentences.n: y kyrchwyt ac ef 'there was a making for (it) with him': kyrchwyt is the impersonal preterite of kyrchu 'make for', and the place gone to, kymwt arall 'another commote', follows with no preposition. A kymwt (cwmwd) is a commote, the division of a cantref. ebolyon 'colts', plural of ebawl. yny 'until'. gwbyl ← cwbyl 'complete', softened in the predicate after uu 'was'. y dal 'his payment' ← tal, softened after y 'his'.

sentences.t: Ac wrth hynny y dodet ar y kymwt hwnnw, o hynny allan, Tal Ebolyon.
sentences.l: And for that was-put on that commote, from that out, Tal Ebolion.
sentences.i: And because of that the commote was called from then on Tal Ebolion.
sentences.n: wrth hynny 'because of that'. y dodet 'was put': dodet is the impersonal preterite of dodi 'put', of the older kind ending -et; to 'put' a name on a place is to give it one. o hynny allan 'from then on'. Tal Ebolyon (in modern spelling Tal Ebolion) is read here as 'payment of colts' (tal 'payment'); the name is the commote of Talebolion in Anglesey, and tal also means 'front, end', so the story may be explaining a name that meant something else.

sentences.t: A'r eil nos, eisted y gyt a wnaethant.
sentences.l: And the second night, sitting together they-did.
sentences.i: And on the second night they sat together.
sentences.n: A'r eil nos 'and the second night': a time phrase, used without a preposition. eil 'second' stands before its noun. eisted y gyt a wnaethant 'sitting together they did', the verbal-noun narrative closed by a wnaethant.

sentences.t: “Arglwyd,” heb y Matholwch, “pan doeth yti y peir a rodeist ymi?”
sentences.l: “Lord,” said Matholwch, “whence came to-you the cauldron that you-gave to-me?”
sentences.i: “Lord,” said Matholwch, “where did the cauldron you gave me come from?”
sentences.n: pan doeth 'whence came': pan here is 'from where', not 'when'. yti 'to you' (itti), ymi 'to me': y conjugated, with the old i and y spellings varying. a rodeist 'that you gave', second-person singular preterite of rodi.

sentences.t: “E doeth im,” heb ef, “y gan wr a uu y'th wlat ti.
sentences.l: “It came to-me,” said he, “from a-man who was in-your country you.
sentences.i: “It came to me,” he said, “from a man who had been in your country.
sentences.n: E doeth 'it came': E = ef 'it', set before the verb as a dummy subject, the abnormal sentence in its smallest form. y gan 'from (the possession of)'. a uu 'who was' ← bu, softened after a. y'th wlat ti 'in your country': y 'in' + 'th 'your'; gwlat softened after 'th, with ti echoing it.

sentences.t: Ac ni wn na bo yno y caffo.”
sentences.l: And I-do-not-know but-that it-may-be there that he-may-have-got-it.”
sentences.i: And for all I know it was there that he got it.”
sentences.n: ni wn 'I do not know' (gwnn, soft after ni). na bo 'that it may not be', with bo the present subjunctive of bot: 'I do not know that it is not there' = it may well be there. y caffo 'that he got (it)': caffo is the present subjunctive of kaffael, kept in the subordinate clause because the whole is uncertain.

sentences.t: “Pwy oed hwnnw?” heb ef.
sentences.l: “Who was that?” said he.
sentences.i: “Who was he?” he said.
sentences.n: Pwy oed hwnnw 'who was that (one)?': hwnnw is the masculine 'that'.

sentences.t: “Llassar Llaes Gyfnewit,” heb ef.
sentences.l: “Llasar Llaes Gyfnewid,” said he.
sentences.i: “Llasar Llaes Gyfnewid,” he said.
sentences.n: Llassar Llaes Gyfnewit, in modern spelling Llasar Llaes Gyfnewid. llassar is a word for blue enamel or azure, and the name has been compared with an Irish one; llaes 'trailing, slack' and kyfnewit 'exchange' make an obscure epithet, and no translation of it is safe. Gyfnewit ← kyfnewit, softened after the adjective llaes.

sentences.t: “A hwnnw a doeth yma o Iwerdon, a Chymidei Kymeinuoll, y wreic, y gyt ac ef, ac a dianghyssant o'r ty hayarn yn Iwerdon pan wnaethpwyt yn wenn yn eu kylch, ac y dianghyssant odyno.
sentences.l: “And that one it-was-that came here from Ireland, and Cymidei Cymeinfoll, his wife, together with-him, and that escaped from the house of-iron in Ireland when it-was-made white around-them, and escaped from-there.
sentences.i: “He came here from Ireland, and Cymidei Cymeinfoll his wife with him; they had escaped from the iron house in Ireland when it was made white-hot about them, and got away from there.
sentences.n: a Chymidei Kymeinuoll ← Kymidei, spirant mutation after a 'and'; the name is Cymidei Cymeinfoll in modern spelling (kymeinuoll has been read as 'big-bellied', but that is uncertain). y wreic 'his wife' ← gwreic, softened after y 'his'. a dianghyssant 'that escaped', third-person plural preterite of dianc. y ty hayarn 'the iron house'. pan wnaethpwyt yn wenn 'when it was made white': wnaethpwyt, the impersonal preterite of gwneuthur, softened after pan; wenn ← gwenn, the feminine of gwynn 'white', softened after yn, as if the speaker thought of a feminine noun (ystauell 'chamber', as the story later calls it); the Red Book has yn wynnyas 'white-heat'. yn eu kylch 'around them'.

sentences.t: Ac eres gynhyf i ony wdosti dim y wrth hynny.”
sentences.l: And strange with-me I if-not you-know anything about that.”
sentences.i: And it would surprise me if you knew nothing of it.”
sentences.n: eres 'strange, a wonder' (gynhyf i 'to me', gan conjugated). ony 'if not'. wdosti = gwdost ti 'you know': gwdost, second-person singular present of gwybot, softened after ony, with ti run into it. dim 'anything'. y wrth 'about, concerning'.

sentences.t: “Gwn, Arglwyd,” heb ef, “a chymeint ac a wnn, mi a'e managaf yti.
sentences.l: “I-know, Lord,” said he, “and as-much as I-know, I it-is-that will-tell-it to-you.
sentences.i: “I do, Lord,” he said, “and as much as I know I will tell you.
sentences.n: Gwn 'I know' answers the question by repeating the verb. a chymeint ac a wnn 'and as much as that I know': spirant after a 'and' (kymeint). mi a'e managaf 'I will tell it': 'e 'it' infixed after a, and managaf, first-person singular present of managu.

sentences.t: Yn hela yd oedwn yn Iwerdon dydgueith ar benn gossed uch penn llyn oed yn Iwerdon, a Llyn y Peir y gelwit.
sentences.l: Hunting I-was in Ireland one-day on top of a-mound above a-lake that-was in Ireland, and the Lake of-the Cauldron it-was-called.
sentences.i: I was hunting in Ireland one day on top of a mound above a lake there, which was called the Lake of the Cauldron.
sentences.n: Yn hela yd oedwn 'hunting I was': a verbal-noun phrase put first for weight, then yd and the verb (first-person singular imperfect of bot). gossed is a readable slip for gorssed 'mound' (the Red Book has gorssed; Evans prints gossed clearly), kept as written: a gorsedd is a mound, often one where marvels are seen. benn ← penn 'top', softened after ar. llyn oed 'a lake (that) was': the relative is left unexpressed. a Llyn y Peir y gelwit 'and the Lake of the Cauldron it was called': gelwit is the impersonal imperfect of galw 'call'. Matholwch's story begins here and runs on to the end of his long speech; the giant's words inside it are marked with single quotes.

sentences.t: A mi a welwn gwr melyngoch mawr, yn dyuot o'r llyn, a pheir ar y geuyn.
sentences.l: And I it-was-that saw a-man yellow-red big, coming from the lake, and a-cauldron on his back.
sentences.i: And I saw a big red-haired man coming out of the lake with a cauldron on his back.
sentences.n: mi a welwn 'I saw', first-person singular imperfect of gwelet. gwr is not softened here, though the object of a verb normally is (wr); the scribe does not always show it. melyngoch 'yellow-red', of the hair or complexion (melyn + coch). a pheir 'and a cauldron': spirant after a. ar y geuyn 'on his back' ← keuyn, softened after y 'his'.

sentences.t: A gwr heuyt athrugar mawr, a drygweith anorles arnaw oed; a gwreic yn y ol; ac ot oed uawr ef, mwy dwyweith oed y wreic noc ef.
sentences.l: And a-man also huge big, and an-evil-look unrestrained on-him it-was; and a-woman after-him; and if he-was big, bigger twice was the woman than he.
sentences.i: He was a huge, great man besides, with a villainous look upon him; and a woman behind him; and if he was big, the woman was twice as big as he.
sentences.n: A gwr heuyt athrugar mawr … oed 'and a man also huge, big … he was': the predicate first, closed by oed at the end of the clause. athrugar 'immense, enormous' (a- + trugar). drygweith anorles is not certainly understood: drygweith is something like 'evil aspect, villainous look' (drwc 'bad'), and anorles may mean 'unrestrained' or the like; the Red Book prints auorles. ac ot oed uawr ef 'and if he was big': ot = o 'if' before a vowel; uawr ← mawr, softened in the predicate. mwy dwyweith 'bigger twice' = twice as big.

sentences.t: A chyrchu ataf a wnaethant, a chyuarch uell im.
sentences.l: And making for-me they-did, and greeting to-me.
sentences.i: And they came up to me and greeted me.
