sentences.n: chyrchu ← kyrchu 'make for', spirant after a. ataf 'to me', at conjugated. chyuarch uell 'greeting': kyuarch gwell, 'to ask better', with gwell written softened, uell (u for w), though an object directly after a verbal noun is not normally softened; the ships' men above greet with guell unsoftened. im 'to me'.

sentences.t: ‘Ie,’ heb y mi, ‘pa gerdet yssyd arnawch chwi?’
sentences.l: ‘Yes,’ said I, ‘what journey is-there on-you you?’
sentences.i: ‘Yes,’ said I, ‘what business are you about?’
sentences.n: heb y mi 'said I'. pa gerdet 'what travelling' ← kerdet, softened after pa: what is your errand? yssyd 'that is', the relative form of bot. arnawch chwi 'on you', ar conjugated, second person plural, with chwi echoing. A journey is 'on' a person as a duty or purpose.

sentences.t: ‘Llyna gerdet yssyd arnam ni, Arglwyd,’ heb ef: ‘y wreic honn,’ heb ef, ‘ym penn pethewnos a mis, y byd beichogi idi, a'r mab a aner yna o'r torllwyth hwnnw, ar benn y pethewnos a'r mi, y byd gwr ymlad llawn aruawc.’
sentences.l: ‘There-is the journey that-is on-us, Lord,’ said he: ‘this woman,’ said he, ‘at the end of a-fortnight and a-month, there-will-be pregnancy to-her, and the son that-may-be-born then of that litter, at the end of the fortnight and the month, there-will-be a-man of-fighting fully armed.’
sentences.i: ‘This is our business, Lord,’ he said. ‘This woman,’ he said, ‘at the end of a fortnight and a month will be brought to bed, and the son born then of that litter will be, at the end of that fortnight and month, a fighting man fully armed.’
sentences.n: Llyna 'there is, that is' (llyma 'here is' with the far demonstrative). ym penn 'at the end of' (yn + penn, the n assimilated). pethewnos 'fortnight', fifteen nights. y byd beichogi idi 'there will be pregnancy to her': in context the term is her delivery, since the son is born then; byd is the future-habitual of bot. a aner 'that may be born': aner is the impersonal present subjunctive of geni. torllwyth 'litter', a word for animals' young, chosen with intent. a'r mi is a readable slip for a'r mis 'and the month' (Evans prints ar mi; the Red Book has armis), kept as written. gwr ymlad 'a man of fighting', a warrior; llawn aruawc 'fully armed'.

sentences.t: Y kymereis inheu wyntwy arnaf, yu gossymdeithaw: y buant ulwydyn gyt a mi.
sentences.l: I-took I-for-my-part them on-me, to maintain-them: they-were a-year with me.
sentences.i: I took them on myself, to keep them; they were with me a year.
sentences.n: Y kymereis 'I took', first-person singular preterite of kymryt, with the particle y. wyntwy 'them' is the emphatic doubled pronoun. arnaf 'on me', as a charge. yu gossymdeithaw 'to maintain them': yu = y 'to' + the infixed 'u 'them'; gossymdeithaw is to keep or provide for. ulwydyn ← blwydyn 'year', softened as an adverb of time.

sentences.t: Yn y ulwydyn y keueis yn diwarauun wynt; o hynny allann y guarauunwyt im.
sentences.l: In the year I-had them without-grudge; from that out it-was-grudged to-me.
sentences.i: For the year I had them with no one's objection; after that I was grudged them.
sentences.n: Yn y ulwydyn 'in the year', the first year; blwydyn softened after the article. y keueis 'I got, I had'. yn diwarauun 'ungrudged': di- 'un-' + gwarafun 'grudge, object to'. y guarauunwyt im 'it was grudged to me': guarauunwyt is the impersonal preterite (-wyt) of gwarafun. o hynny allann 'from then on'.

sentences.t: A chyn penn y pedwyryd mis wynt eu hun yn peri eu hatcassu, ac anghynwys yn y wlat, yn gwneuthur sarahedeu, ac yn eighaw ac yn gouudyaw guyrda a gwragedda.
sentences.l: And before the end of the fourth month they themselves causing their being-hated, and unwelcome in the land, doing outrages, and molesting and vexing noblemen and noblewomen.
sentences.i: And before the end of the fourth month they had made themselves hated and unwelcome in the land, committing outrages, and molesting and harassing noblemen and noblewomen.
sentences.n: mis 'month' is supplied from the Red Book: the White Book has no word after pedwyryd 'fourth', which has nothing to count without it. The sentence has no finite verb: wynt eu hun yn peri 'they themselves causing'. eu hatcassu 'their being hated': eu 'their' puts h before a vowel; atcassu is to hate, or to make hated. anghynwys 'unwelcome, not to be borne' (an- + kynwys 'admit'). sarahedeu 'insults, outrages', plural of sarhaet. eighaw is taken as 'molest, ill-treat', a rare word; gouudyaw 'vex, afflict' (gofidio). guyrda 'noblemen'; gwragedda 'noblewomen' (the plural of gwreicda).

sentences.t: O hynny allan y dygyuores uyg kyuoeth am ym pen y erchi im ymuadeu ac wynt, a rodi dewis im, ae uyg kyuoeth ae wynt.
sentences.l: From that out rose-up my realm about my head to ask of-me renouncing with them, and giving a-choice to-me, either my realm or them.
sentences.i: From then on my realm rose up against me, demanding that I part with them, and giving me a choice: my realm or them.
sentences.n: y dygyuores 'rose up, mustered': dygyuores is the third-person singular preterite of dygyuor 'gather, rise'. uyg kyuoeth 'my realm': uyg is uy 'my' with the nasal mutation shown on the possessive (the noun would be nghyuoeth in modern spelling). am ym pen 'about my head', against me. y erchi im 'to ask of me' (erchi 'demand'). ymuadeu ac 'renounce, give up' (ymwadu â). ae … ae 'either … or'.

sentences.t: E dodeis inheu ar gynghor uy gwlat beth a wneit amdanunt.
sentences.l: I put I-for-my-part (it) to the counsel of-my country what would-be-done about-them.
sentences.i: I put it to the council of my country what should be done about them.
sentences.n: E dodeis 'I put': E is the preverbal particle (= ef), and dodeis the first-person singular preterite of dodi. inheu 'I for my part'. uy gwlat 'my country': the nasal mutation after uy is not shown (ngwlat). beth ← peth 'what', softened. a wneit 'would be done', impersonal imperfect of gwneuthur. amdanunt 'about them', am conjugated.

sentences.t: Nyd eynt wy o'y bod; nit oed reit udunt wynteu oc eu hanuod, herwyd ymlad, uynet.
sentences.l: They-would-not-go they of their will; it-was-not need for-them they against their will, by fighting, to-go.
sentences.i: They would not go of their own will, and they need not go against it, for nobody could fight them out.
sentences.n: Nyd eynt 'they would not go': eynt is the third-person plural imperfect of mynet (aent). o'y bod 'of their will': bod 'will, consent', with 'y as 'their'. nit oed reit udunt … uynet 'there was no necessity for them to go': uynet ← mynet, held back to the end. oc eu hanuod 'against their will' (oc = o 'of' before a vowel; h before a vowel after eu). herwyd ymlad 'by way of fighting': they could not be forced out, so huge were they.

sentences.t: Ac yna yn y kyuyng gynghor, y causant gwneuthur ystauell haearn oll;
sentences.l: And then in the narrow counsel, they-got making a-chamber of-iron all;
sentences.i: And then, at their wits' end, they decided to make a chamber all of iron;
sentences.n: yn y kyuyng gynghor 'in the narrow counsel', in that strait: kyuyng 'narrow' stands before its noun and softens it (kynghor > gynghor). y causant 'they got', third-person plural preterite of kaffael: their counsel came out with a plan. gwneuthur is not softened as the object here. ystauell 'chamber, room'; haearn oll 'all iron'. The sentence runs on through the next two units.

sentences.t: a gwedy bot y barawt yr ystauell, dyuyn a oed o of yn Iwerdon yno, o'r a oed o perchen geuel a mwrthwl,
sentences.l: and after being ready the chamber, summoning all that was of smith in Ireland there, of-all that was of owner of-tongs and hammer,
sentences.i: and when the chamber was ready, every smith in Ireland was summoned there, every man who owned tongs and hammer,
sentences.n: gwedy bot y barawt yr ystauell 'after the chamber was ready': y barawt is yn barawt (the Red Book has yn), parawt softened after the predicative yn. dyuyn 'summoning' (dyfynnu). a oed o of 'what there was of smith': of ← gof 'smith', softened after o. o'r a oed 'of all who were'. o perchen 'of owner': perchen is not softened after o here (the Red Book has oberchen). geuel 'tongs' (gefel); mwrthwl 'hammer'.

sentences.t: a pheri gossot kyuuch a chrib yr ystauell o lo, a pheri guassanaethu yn diwall o uwyt a llyn arnunt, ar y wreic, a'y gwr, a'y phlant.
sentences.l: and causing setting as-high-as the ridge of-the chamber of charcoal, and causing serving without-stint of food and drink upon-them, on the woman, and her husband, and her children.
sentences.i: and they had charcoal piled as high as the roof of the chamber, and had the woman and her husband and her children served with food and drink without stint.
sentences.n: a pheri 'and causing': peri + verbal noun is 'have (something) done'. gossot 'setting, placing'. kyuuch a 'as high as': kyuuch is the equative of uchel. chrib ← crib 'crest, ridge', the roof-ridge, spirant after a. o lo 'of charcoal' ← glo, softened after o. guassanaethu arnunt 'to serve them' (gwasanaethu ar). yn diwall 'without lack, abundantly'. llyn here is 'drink', not 'lake'. a'y phlant 'and her children': 'y 'her' brings the spirant mutation (plant > phlant), which tells you whose children they are.

sentences.t: A phan wybuwyt eu medwi wynteu, y dechreuwyt kymyscu y tan a'r glo am ben yr ystauell, a chwythu y megineu a oed wedy eu gossot yg kylch y ty, a gwr a pob dwy uegin, a dechreu chwythu y megineu yny uyd y ty yn burwen am eu penn.
sentences.l: And when was-known their being-drunk they-for-their-part, was-begun mixing the fire and the charcoal about the top of the chamber, and blowing the bellows that were after their setting around the house, and a-man with every two bellows, and beginning to-blow the bellows until is the house white-hot about their head.
sentences.i: And when it was known that they were drunk, they began to mix the fire and the charcoal over the top of the chamber, and to blow the bellows that had been set round the house, a man to every two bellows; and the bellows were blown until the house was white-hot about them.
sentences.n: wybuwyt ← gwybuwyt, the impersonal preterite of gwybot 'know', softened after pan; dechreuwyt, the impersonal preterite of dechreu 'begin'. eu medwi 'their getting drunk' (meddwi). am ben 'about the top of' ← penn, softened after am. a oed wedy eu gossot 'that were after their setting' = had been set. yg kylch 'around' (yng nghylch, the nasal shown only on yn). a gwr a pob dwy uegin 'and a man with every two bellows': megin softened after dwy; after a 'with' one expects phob, but the scribe writes pob. yny uyd 'until it is': a present tense, as in the pilot's ual y byd, for a vivid moment. burwen 'pure white' (pur + gwen).

sentences.t: Ac yna y bu y kynghor ganthunt hwy ymherued llawr yr ystauell; ac yd arhoes ef yny uyd y pleit haearn yn wenn.
sentences.l: And then was the counsel with-them they in-the-middle of-the floor of-the chamber; and he-waited he until is the wall of-iron white.
sentences.i: And then they held council in the middle of the chamber floor; and he waited until the iron wall was white.
sentences.n: y bu y kynghor ganthunt 'the counsel was with them' = they held a council: ganthunt is gan conjugated, third person plural. ymherued 'in the middle of' (yn + perued, with the nasal mutation). yd arhoes 'waited', third-person singular preterite of aros (arhoi). pleit 'wall, side, partition'. yny uyd again: 'until it is'.

sentences.t: Ac rac diruawr wres, y kyrchwys y bleit a'e yscwyd a'y tharaw gantaw allan, ac yn y ol ynteu y wreic.
sentences.l: And for huge heat, he-made-for the wall with his shoulder and striking-it with-him out, and after-him he-for-his-part his wife.
sentences.i: And for the great heat he charged the wall with his shoulder and burst it out, and his wife after him.
sentences.n: rac 'for, because of'. wres ← gwres 'heat', softened after diruawr 'huge'. y kyrchwys 'made for, charged', third-person singular preterite of kyrchu. y bleit ← pleit, feminine, softened after the article. a'e yscwyd 'with his shoulder'. a'y tharaw 'and striking it': 'y 'her, it' refers to the feminine pleit and brings the spirant mutation (taraw > tharaw). gantaw allan 'out with him', so that it went out before him. yn y ol ynteu y wreic 'after him his wife', with no verb.

sentences.t: A neb ny dieghis odyna namyn ef a'e wreic.
sentences.l: And no-one did-not-escape from-there except him and his wife.
sentences.i: And no one escaped from there but he and his wife.
sentences.n: neb ny dieghis 'no one escaped': Welsh doubles the negative, neb with ny; dieghis is the third-person singular preterite (-is) of dianc. odyna 'from there'. namyn 'but, except'.

sentences.t: Ac yna o'm tebygu i, Arglwyd,” heb y Matholwch wrth Uendigeiduran, “y doeth ef drwod attat ti.”
sentences.l: And then, by-my supposing I, Lord,” said Matholwch to Bendigeidfran, “he-came he across to-you.”
sentences.i: And then, as I suppose, Lord,” said Matholwch to Bendigeidfran, “he came over to you.”
sentences.n: o'm tebygu i 'by my supposing': o + 'm 'my', with the verbal noun tebygu. heb y Matholwch wrth Uendigeiduran 'said Matholwch to Bendigeidfran': wrth 'to', softening the name. drwod 'across, over' (drosodd). attat ti 'to you', at conjugated. Here Matholwch's long speech ends.

sentences.t: “Yna dioer,” heb ynteu, “y doeth yma, ac y roes y peir y minheu.”
sentences.l: “Then assuredly,” said he-for-his-part, “he-came here, and he-gave the cauldron to me.”
sentences.i: “Then indeed,” he said, “he came here, and he gave the cauldron to me.”
sentences.n: Yna … y doeth yma 'then … he came here': the time adverb first, then the verb with y. y roes 'gave', third-person singular preterite of rodi (rhoes). y minheu 'to me for my part': y 'to' with the emphatic pronoun.

sentences.t: “Pa delw, Arglwyd, yd erbynneisti wynteu?”
sentences.l: “What manner, Lord, did-you-receive them?”
sentences.i: “And how, Lord, did you receive them?”
sentences.n: Pa delw 'what form, in what way?' (delw 'image, form'), then yd and the verb. erbynneisti = erbynneist ti, the second-person singular preterite of erbyn 'receive', with ti run into it. wynteu 'them for their part'.

sentences.t: “Eu rannu ym pob lle yn y kyuoeth, ac y maent yn lluossauc, ac yn dyrchauael ym pob lle, ac yn cadarnhau y uann y bythont, o wyr ac arueu goreu a welas neb.”
sentences.l: “Their dividing in every place in the realm, and they-are numerous, and rising in every place, and fortifying the place where they-are, with men and arms the-best that anyone saw.”
sentences.i: “I dispersed them in every part of the realm, and they are many, and they are thriving everywhere, and fortifying every place they settle in with the best men and arms that anyone ever saw.”
sentences.n: Eu rannu 'their dividing': the verbal noun with eu 'their' as its object, used as a past answer without a finite verb. y maent 'they are'. yn lluossauc 'numerous' (lluosog). yn dyrchauael 'rising', prospering. cadarnhau 'strengthen, fortify'. y uann ← mann 'place', softened after the article. y bythont 'where they are (wont to be)': bythont is a third-person plural consuetudinal present of bot; the Red Book has y bont. goreu a welas neb 'the best that anyone saw': welas ← gwelas, third-person singular preterite of gwelet.

about: Bendigeidfran son of Llŷr, crowned king of the Island of the Mighty, is sitting on the rock of Harlech with his brother Manawydan and his half-brothers Nisien the peacemaker and Efnysien the maker of quarrels, when thirteen ships come from the south of Ireland with a shield raised point-upward in sign of peace, bringing Matholwch, king of Ireland, to ask for Branwen daughter of Llŷr so that Ireland and the Island of the Mighty may be bound together. The council grants her, and Matholwch sleeps with her at Aberffraw, where the feast is held in pavilions because no house has ever held Bendigeidfran; but Efnysien, angry that his sister was given away without his leave, maims Matholwch's horses, and Matholwch, told that it was done to shame him, makes for his ships. Bendigeidfran sends after him twice, the second time with Manawydan and an offer of a sound horse for every one spoiled, a rod of silver as thick and as long as himself, a plate of gold as broad as his face, and peace on his own terms; Matholwch's council judges that refusing is likelier to bring shame than amends, and he comes back, is paid in horses and in colts (whence, the tale says, the commote's name Tal Ebolion), and, still downcast, is given a cauldron that brings a man killed one day back by the next, though without speech. On the second night Matholwch tells where the cauldron came from: the huge Llasar Llaes Gyfnewid and his wife Cymidei Cymeinfoll, twice his size, came out of the Lake of the Cauldron in Ireland, made themselves hated there, and broke out of an iron chamber heated white around them; Bendigeidfran answers that Llasar came to him and gave him the cauldron, and that he has spread them through his realm, where they multiply and fortify every place they hold.
